In Mongolia, Buryatia and Kalmykia every nomadic household traditionally kept an Ikhel in the yurt and used it to accompany the Jangar epic at night. In the Soviet period Tuva tried to "modernise" the igil to bring it closer to the European cello, but most Tuvan musicians today still play an instrument and style that largely keep the original form. Igil is a two-string bowed instrument of Mongolia and Tuva, a chordophone, H-S number 321.322-71. The neck and lute-shaped soundbox are usually carved from a single piece of pine or larch, and the soundboard may be covered with skin or a thin wooden plate; the strings and bow hair are traditionally horsehair, or nylon, and the head is often carved as a horse's head. In playing the body stands nearly upright, with the soundbox on the leg or braced against the top of a boot, and the strings are touched with the fingernail or fingertip rather than pressed to the neck; there are no frets and the bow is held underhand. Nomadic households in Mongolia, Buryatia and Kalmykia traditionally keep this instrument in the yurt and use it to accompany the Jangar epic at night; musicians in Tuva today mostly still use the original form.

演奏伊吉勒馬頭琴時，琴身近乎直立，共鳴箱置於膝上，或抵住靴頂固定。發聲以弓擦弦，: In playing the igil the body is held nearly upright and the soundbox rests on the knee or is braced against the top of a boot. Sound is made by rubbing the strings with the bow, held underhand. The strings are touched with the fingernail or fingertip and are not pressed towards the neck, and the instrument has no frets. A beginner can first steady the hold, then practise the underhand bow grip and lightly touching the two parallel strings, and finally combine bowing so that the strings vibrate.
